questions.explanation: BERDE is appropriate for domestic projects and government buildings, but the scenario explicitly states '20% improvement' which is EDGE's defining metric. LEED has global prestige but uses a point-based system with varying thresholds, not a fixed 20% improvement target. ISO 14001 is an environmental management system, not a building performance certification. EDGE, administered by the IFC, is specifically designed around a 20% improvement target in energy, water, and embodied energy. It is cost-effective and accessible to developing economies, making it ideal for IFC-funded projects. EDGE is the IFC's efficiency-focused certification system; 20% improvement is its defining metric.

questions.explanation: Incorrect—prerequisites are mandatory, not optional. Incorrect—prerequisites cannot be bypassed with credits. All BERDE certified projects must meet all prerequisites. Incorrect—BERDE explicitly uses prerequisites. BERDE structure: Prerequisites in Energy, Water, Site, Materials, and Waste are non-negotiable baseline performance levels. Optional credits allow projects to exceed baseline and achieve higher star ratings (1–5 stars). This two-tiered approach ensures minimum sustainability; optional credits reward innovation. BERDE uses a prerequisite (mandatory) + credit (optional advancement) model, similar to LEED. All certified projects must pass prerequisites.

questions.explanation: Renewable energy installation is desirable and can earn points, but it is not a mandatory prerequisite; many projects achieve BERDE without on-site PV. Green roofs are an innovation strategy, not a prerequisite; they are optional. Rainwater harvesting is one strategy to meet Water Efficiency prerequisite, but the prerequisite itself (potable water reduction) is mandatory; the implementation strategy varies. Water Efficiency is a mandatory BERDE prerequisite; all projects must demonstrate minimum potable water reduction targets. This reflects the Philippines' water management challenges, especially in high-precipitation regions. BERDE prerequisites are mandatory minimum performance levels; Water Efficiency, Energy Efficiency, Site Selection, Materials, and Waste Management are all required categories.

questions.explanation: High-efficiency AC is important but cannot replace the energy savings of passive design in tropical climates. Relying on mechanical systems increases operational costs and vulnerability to power outages (common in monsoon season). LED lighting reduces lighting energy (typically 10–15% of total), but climate control (heating/cooling) dominates office energy consumption (~40–60%). Addressing the larger load is more impactful. Double-glazing in tropical climates is less critical than in cold climates; it may increase cost without proportional benefit. Solar shading and ventilation are more cost-effective. In the Philippines' hot, humid climate, passive design—natural ventilation, orientation to catch prevailing breezes (NE/SW in many regions), solar shading (deep overhangs, louvers), and thermal mass (exposed concrete ceilings)—dramatically reduces cooling load. This is more cost-effective than active systems and improves resilience. Tropical climate design must prioritize passive cooling (ventilation, shading, mass) before active systems. This aligns with BERDE's emphasis on climate-responsive design.
